To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the redox-regulation and oxidative stress is a critical factor for the regulation of estrogen and estrogen metabolizing proteins in gynecological-cancer.
the oxidative-stress can induce redox-regulation and thereby modulates estrogen-metabolizing proteins and thereby influence the estrogen-signalling in female reproductive-organa.
oxidative stress can modulate estrogen-signalling by affecting the expression/activity of ER, SULT, STS and FGEE.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the role of oxidative stress in the regulation of estrogen-signalling.
the identification of new targets for therapeutic intervention in gynecological-cancer treatment.
the role of oxidative-stress in estrogen-signalling and may provide new insights to treat gynaecological cancers.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
oxidative-stress and estrogen are two sides of the same coin and both are equally important in the development of gynaecologic-cancers.
oxidative-stress may be an important determinant of estrogen signalling in gynaecological cancers.
oxidative-threats can influence estrogen-signalling via redox-regulation and vice-versa.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the redox regulation of the estrogen-signalling is a critical determinant in the development of gynecological-cancer.
oxidative-threats are important determinants in the pathogenesis and progression of gynaecologic-cancers and the redox-regulation may be a critical factor that influences E2 signalling.
estrogen and oxidative-stress are interlinked and both are important determinants of gynaecologic-cancers.
The main takeaway from our work is that
redox regulation of ER/SULT1E1/STS and FGE may play an important role in the pathogenesis/progression of gynecological-cancer.
oxidative-stress may influence estrogen-signalling via regulating ER, STS and SULT1E.
oxidative-threats are important determinants of E2-signalling in gynaecological cancers.
